pages.answer: Twice as tall, and each cycle takes half the time
pages.name: Still there?
options: Just as tall, but each cycle takes half the time
Twice as tall, and each cycle takes half the time
Twice as tall, with cycles as long as before
pages.task: A coil spins steadily in a magnet's field and makes an AC wave. Now it spins twice as fast. What happens to its wave?
pages.why: Each turn makes one cycle. So twice the speed packs twice the cycles into each second, and each takes half the time. The flux through the coil also changes twice as fast. So the wave stands twice as tall. Speed moves both together. The alternator here does the same, with the magnet turning instead of the coil.

pages.text: The rotor is a magnet with one north and one south pole. It turns inside the fixed stator. The coils stay still, so the big output currents leave through fixed connections. As the north pole and then the south pole pass coil A, its trace makes one full cycle. That happens once every turn.

pages.alt: An alternator seen end on. A rotor with 2 poles, north and south in turn, sits inside a fixed stator. Coil A is at the top; the places for coils B and C are empty. Field arrows run out of each north pole and round into the next south pole. The rotor is still. A trace shows coil A's voltage against time over 60 ms, with a dashed line, marked full field, where each wave peaks at full field and 60 Hz. The traces run flat at zero.
pages.answer: None, because the flux through it is not changing
pages.name: A parked pole
options: Its biggest, because the flux through it is strongest
A steady direct voltage, because the field current is direct
None, because the flux through it is not changing
pages.task: The rotor stops with its north pole square in front of coil A. The field current is still on. What voltage does coil A make?
pages.why: A coil makes voltage only while the flux through it changes. A parked pole gives coil A plenty of flux, but the flux is steady. So coil A makes nothing until the rotor turns again.

pages.alt: An alternator seen end on. A rotor with 2 poles, north and south in turn, sits inside a fixed stator. The stator carries 3 coils, A, B and C in turn, 120° apart. Field arrows run out of each north pole and round into the next south pole. The rotor is still. Three traces, A, B and C, show each coil's voltage against time over 60 ms, with a dashed line, marked full field, where each wave peaks at full field and 60 Hz. The three waves have the same shape, each 120° behind the last.
pages.name: Three coils, three phases
pages.text: Coils B and C sit 120° round the stator from A and from each other. Each pole reaches them a third of a turn later. So three equal waves build, each 120° behind the one before. Each coil lights up as the gap between two poles passes it, where its flux changes fastest.

pages.name: B behind A
pages.task: A 2-pole rotor turns at 3000 rev/min. Coil B sits 120° on from coil A, in the direction the rotor turns. How long after coil A's wave peaks does coil B's wave peak?
pages.why: 3000 rev/min is 3000 ÷ 60 = 50 turns a second. So one turn takes 1 ÷ 50 s, which is 20 ms. Coil B is a third of a turn on. So its wave peaks 20 ÷ 3 = 6.67 ms after A's.

pages.alt: An alternator seen end on. A rotor with 4 poles, north and south in turn, sits inside a fixed stator. The stator carries 6 coils, A, B and C in turn, 60° apart. pages.name: Two pole pairs
pages.text: A 4-pole rotor has two pole pairs. Coil A sees a north and a south go by twice each turn. So it makes two full cycles a turn. The stator carries a set of three coils for each pole pair, 60° apart. A pole pair passes in half a turn, so 60° of rotor is 120° of wave.

pages.name: Cycles in a turn
pages.task: A 6-pole rotor makes one full turn. How many full cycles does coil A make?
pages.why: 6 poles make 3 pole pairs, each a north and a south. Each pair sweeping past coil A makes one cycle. So one turn makes 3.

pages.name: Speed sets frequency
pages.text: Frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. A 2-pole machine makes 60 Hz at 3600 rev/min. A 4-pole one makes it at 1800 rev/min. The rule is also printed as f = P × N ÷ 120, where P counts poles.

pages.alt: An alternator seen end on. A rotor with 4 poles, north and south in turn, sits inside a fixed stator. The stator carries 6 coils, A, B and C in turn, 60° apart. The three waves have the same shape, each 120° behind the last.
pages.name: A 4-pole set
pages.task: A 4-pole set turns at 1800 rev/min. What frequency does it make?
pages.why: 4 poles make 2 pole pairs. So 2 × 1800 ÷ 60 = 60 Hz. The poles form gives 4 × 1800 ÷ 120 = 60 Hz. Both forms agree when P means what each one says.

pages.alt: An alternator seen end on. A rotor with 4 poles, north and south in turn, sits inside a fixed stator. The stator carries 6 coils, A, B and C in turn, 60° apart. The three waves have the same shape, each 120° behind the last.
pages.name: Speed or field
pages.text: Take a 4-pole set with nothing connected and the field unchanged. Slowed 5%, from 1800 to 1710 rev/min, its waves get both lower and less frequent: 57 Hz and 418 V. Turning the field current down shrinks the waves but leaves them at 60 Hz.

pages.name: Back to 60 Hz
options: Either one, since both change the waves
pages.task: A set running alone on its board reads 58 Hz. What brings it back to 60 Hz?
pages.why: Frequency = pole pairs × rev/min ÷ 60. The field is nowhere in that rule. So only the speed changes the frequency. The voltage comes back up with the speed.

pages.name: A slow 6-pole set
pages.task: A 6-pole set with nothing connected makes 440 V at 60 Hz. Its engine slows to 1080 rev/min. The field current stays the same. What voltage does it make now?
pages.why: 6 poles are 3 pole pairs. So the frequency is 3 × 1080 ÷ 60 = 54 Hz. With the field unchanged, the voltage falls in step: 440 × 54 ÷ 60 = 396 V.

pages.name: Speed for 50 Hz
pages.task: What speed must a 6-pole alternator turn at to make 50 Hz?
pages.why: 6 poles are 3 pole pairs. So rev/min = 50 × 60 ÷ 3 = 1000. As a check, 3 × 1000 ÷ 60 = 50 Hz.
